outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the comprehensive survey on LLM Security. This section will outline the rapid evolution of the threat landscape from 2023 to 2026, highlighting the transition from static, unimodal vulnerabilities to dynamic, multimodal, and agentic attack vectors. It will briefly touch upon the four core categories analyzed: Data and Model Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and LLM Hallucinations, summarizing the shift toward automated adversarial optimization and the corresponding need for co-evolutionary defense mechanisms.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: This section establishes the motivation, scope, and contributions of the survey. It will detail the critical transition in LLM security between 2023 and 2026, moving from the identification of baseline vulnerabilities in isolated models to a highly sophisticated arms race involving multimodal and agentic systems. The introduction will outline the survey's structure, explicitly mapping the trajectory from training-time threats (poisoning) to inference-time vulnerabilities (adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations). It will emphasize the paradigm shift from static, rule-based guardrails to dynamic, automated adversarial optimization.

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section provides the foundational concepts and definitions required for the survey, strictly adhering to standard LLM security terminology. It will define key concepts such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Red Teaming. It will also establish a unified threat model taxonomy, distinguishing between black-box and white-box attacker capabilities, and differentiating between training-time access (data poisoning, backdoors) and inference-time access (adversarial suffixes, prompt manipulation). The section will avoid forcing specific empirical citations here, focusing instead on establishing a rigorous conceptual framework.

outline.title: 3. Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: This section explores the 2024-2025 evolution of data and model poisoning attacks. It will begin by detailing the 2024 foundational benchmarking of generative backdoors in open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-2, Mistral, GPT-J), specifically citing the frameworks established by [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. The narrative will then transition to the late 2024/2025 shift toward complex, multimodal, and embodied AI attack vectors. A critical focus will be the exploitation of alignment and retrieval mechanisms, demonstrating how the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline—traditionally a safety mechanism—has emerged as a novel vulnerability surface for sophisticated poisoning campaigns.

outline.title: 4. Inference-Time Threats: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: This section details the rapid evolution of adversarial attacks on LLMs and MLLMs from 2024 to 2026. It will start by examining the 2024 baseline vulnerabilities in high-stakes, specialized domains, specifically referencing [Yang_2024_Adversarial] to illustrate the susceptibility of models processing sensitive healthcare datasets like MIMIC-III. The section will then trace the trajectory from these domain-specific exploits to a highly sophisticated, multi-faceted arms race characterized by advanced offensive weaponization. It will cover how attackers transitioned from simple input perturbations to complex, mathematically optimized adversarial suffixes designed to systematically degrade model performance and bypass domain-specific safety filters.

outline.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section focuses on the 2025-2026 transformative shift in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, highlighting the move from manual, rule-based exploits to automated, co-evolutionary adversarial optimization. It will detail how attackers successfully automated the discovery of adversarial prompts using modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms. The section must cite [Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM], and [Maloyan_2025_LLM] to discuss the alarming Attack Success Rates (ASR) of 50% to 71% achieved against state-of-the-art LLM agents. It will also explore the bifurcation of offensive research into extreme computational efficiency versus dynamic, ensemble-based attack systems.

outline.title: 6. Model Reliability and Factual Security: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: This section frames LLM hallucinations as a critical reliability and security overlap, tracing its research evolution from 2023 to 2026. It will begin with the 2023 urgent need for baseline detection, highlighting zero-shot inference-time methods. Specifically, it will cite the introduction of ChainPoll by [Friel_2023_LLM], demonstrating how LLM-based polling and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting optimized inference costs while outperforming contemporary competitors. The narrative will then cover the 2024 conceptual maturation, where the field moved beyond treating non-factual generations as simple binary errors, advancing toward highly optimized, mechanistically informed frameworks for ensuring factual consistency in high-stakes deployments.

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms developed between 2024 and 2026 to counter the aforementioned threats. It will begin with early 2024 'patchwork' approaches, such as external stateful detection and prompt-level manipulations, specifically citing [Wang_2024_Advqdet] for its introduction of contrastive prompt tuning to detect query-based black-box attacks with up to 99% efficacy. The section will then trace the evolution toward integrated, dynamic, and ensemble-based defensive systems required to mitigate automated optimization attacks (e.g., GCG, MCTS) and complex multimodal poisoning, highlighting the ongoing co-evolutionary arms race between attackers and defenders.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: This MANDATORY section synthesizes the evaluation frameworks, benchmarks, datasets, and metrics utilized across all four threat categories. It will detail how the community measures Attack Success Rate (ASR) in automated jailbreaks ([Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM]), evaluates generative backdoors in open-source models ([Chowdhury_2024_Breaking], [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]), and assesses factual consistency/hallucinations using LLM-as-a-judge paradigms ([Friel_2023_LLM]). The section will critically analyze the shift from static benchmarks (e.g., AdvBench) to dynamic, agentic evaluation environments, and discuss the trade-offs between computational cost metrics and detection efficacy in modern red-teaming pipelines.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section synthesizes the critical gaps and limitations in the current state of LLM security research. It will discuss the fundamental inadequacy of static guardrails against adaptive, automated optimization techniques. It will also highlight the open challenges in securing multimodal and embodied AI systems, the inherent vulnerabilities within RLHF alignment pipelines, and the difficulty of balancing computational efficiency with robust hallucination detection. The section will propose future research directions, emphasizing the need for mechanistically interpretable defenses and resilient alignment strategies.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: The final section will provide a definitive synthesis of the survey's findings. It will reiterate the central thesis: the LLM security landscape has rapidly transitioned from isolated, unimodal vulnerabilities to a highly automated, multimodal arms race. The conclusion will summarize the key takeaways across data poisoning, adversarial attacks, prompt injection, and hallucinations, and offer practical, actionable recommendations for AI deployers, policymakers, and the academic research community to foster safer foundation models.

background_and_preliminaries.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
background_and_preliminaries.text:
### 2.1 Safety Alignment and its Limitations

Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse applications, yet their deployment in critical and sensitive domains—such as chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) research—raises significant security concerns regarding potential misuse [Li_2025_LLM]. To mitigate these risks, models are typically equipped with built-in safeguards through a process known as safety alignment, which aims to ensure that LLMs behave according to human values and intentions [Wang_2026_LLM]. This alignment is standardly achieved via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by advanced reinforcement learning techniques [Li_2025_LLM].

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become the dominant approach for safety alignment, training models to produce outputs that are preferred by human annotators [Wang_2026_LLM]. Extensions of this paradigm, such as Safe RLHF, explicitly decouple helpfulness and harmlessness objectives, while Constitutional AI leverages AI-generated feedback to scale the alignment process [Wang_2026_LLM]. Furthermore, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies the alignment pipeline by directly optimizing for human preferences without the necessity of explicit reward modeling [Wang_2026_LLM]. Despite these robust methodologies, current alignment approaches exhibit fundamental limitations. Recent studies reveal that alignment is often superficial, affecting only the first few output tokens, and that even benign fine-tuning can inadvertently compromise model safety [Wang_2026_LLM]. Additionally, safety-aligned models possess fragile modes that adversaries can easily trigger to bypass established safeguards [Wang_2026_LLM].

### 2.2 Threat Model Taxonomy

To systematically understand and mitigate LLM vulnerabilities, it is necessary to establish a comprehensive threat model taxonomy that categorizes attacks based on the adversary's access level and the targeted phase of the model lifecycle [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Threat models are broadly bifurcated into training-time and inference-time attacks.

Training-time attacks manipulate the foundational behavior of the model before deployment. A primary vector in this category is data poisoning, which corrupts the model's training or alignment data [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. For example, clean-label poisoning attacks can exploit vulnerabilities in multi-modal RLHF pipelines. The BADREWARD attack demonstrates this by inducing visual feature collisions in reward models, corrupting reward signals without altering preference annotations, thereby steering text-to-image generation toward harmful outputs [Duan_2025_RLHF]. Another severe training-time threat is the backdoor attack, which embeds hidden triggers into the model. Recent frameworks formulate backdoor injection as a lightweight knowledge editing problem, directly altering a minimal subset of LLM parameters to inject robust backdoors that persist even after subsequent fine-tuning [Li_2024_Badedit]. Notably, while integrating poisoned data may not markedly degrade overall model performance on standard medical benchmarks, it can lead to noticeable shifts in fine-tuned model weights, providing a potential pathway for detection [Yang_2024_Adversarial].

Inference-time attacks, conversely, aim to manipulate the outputs of an already deployed model [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. The capabilities of the attacker during inference are classified into white-box and black-box settings. White-box attackers possess full access to the model's internal architecture, weights, and gradients. Black-box attackers, however, operate without internal access, relying solely on querying the model. Executing systematic attacks against black-box agents is challenging due to architectural complexity, often requiring advanced fuzzing frameworks that utilize adaptive seed scoring and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithms to automate the generation of adversarial prompts [Wang_2025_LLM].

### 2.3 Jailbreaks, Prompt Injection, and Attack Success Rate (ASR)

A primary mechanism for inference-time exploitation is the jailbreak attack. Jailbreaks are sophisticated prompting techniques designed specifically to bypass a model's built-in safeguards and elicit harmful or unethical responses [Li_2025_LLM]. The effectiveness of these attacks, and the corresponding robustness of defenses, is quantitatively measured using the Attack Success Rate (ASR), which represents the percentage of adversarial prompts that successfully bypass safety alignment [Zhan_2025_LLM]. Jailbreaking methodologies have evolved from manual prompt engineering to automated approaches that harness LLMs to generate adversarial examples and jailbreak instructions [Slms_2025_Efficient]. To overcome the deployment complexities of using large models for attack generation, recent research has introduced adversarial prompt distillation, a framework that integrates masked language modeling and reinforcement learning to transfer LLM jailbreaking capabilities into smaller language models (SLMs) [Slms_2025_Efficient].

Closely related to jailbreaks is prompt injection, which involves inserting malicious instructions to alter the model's intended evaluation or generation behavior. In the context of evaluation pipelines, prompt injection threats are explicitly distinguished into two models: Content-Author Attacks and System-Prompt Attacks [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. In a Content-Author Attack, a malicious user submits text containing adversarial elements that passes through the evaluation pipeline unchanged, targeting the judge's assessment of user-generated content [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. In a System-Prompt Attack, the adversary targets the template instructions used by the LLM judge, attempting to compromise the evaluation pipeline itself [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. The disruptor components of these attacks typically include direct command injection to override processes, output manipulation to force predetermined scores, and context nullification to ignore original evaluation criteria [Maloyan_2025_LLM].

Furthermore, as LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents interacting with external environments, they become highly susceptible to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) attacks [Zhan_2025_LLM]. In IPI scenarios, adversarial instructions are not provided directly by the user but are embedded within external tools or retrieved documents, posing severe security risks that necessitate adaptive attack evaluations to uncover vulnerabilities in current defenses [Zhan_2025_LLM].

### 2.4 Theoretical Foundations of Prompt Vulnerabilities

The susceptibility of LLMs to jailbreaks and prompt injections can be understood through several theoretical frameworks from cognitive science and machine learning. The attention sink phenomenon reveals that initial tokens in a prompt receive disproportionately high attention weights regardless of semantic relevance due to softmax normalization constraints, indicating that prompt position significantly impacts token influence [Wang_2026_LLM]. This is further supported by position bias and the "lost in the middle" phenomenon, which demonstrates that LLMs exhibit a U-shaped retrieval accuracy curve, with significantly degraded performance for information located in the middle of long contexts [Wang_2026_LLM].

Additionally, instruction hierarchy theory formalizes how LLMs prioritize conflicting instructions from different privilege levels, revealing that societal authority framings often override explicit system or user distinctions [Wang_2026_LLM]. From a cognitive perspective, dual process theory distinguishes between fast, intuitive System 1 processing and slow, deliberative System 2 reasoning, providing insights into why reasoning-enhanced models exhibit different safety characteristics [Wang_2026_LLM]. Finally, Bayesian inference models propose that transformers perform in-context learning through implicit Bayesian inference, where few-shot examples update the model's posterior distribution over possible tasks, mathematically explaining how demonstrations can shift model behavior and interact with prompt-based defenses [Wang_2026_LLM].

### 2.5 Defense Mechanisms and Red Teaming

Defending against the diverse landscape of LLM attacks requires a comprehensive suite of mitigation strategies. Current approaches encompass data filtering, the implementation of guardrails, robust training techniques, adversarial training, and safety context distillation [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking]. Prompt-based defenses, such as Role-Oriented Prompts (RoP) and Task-Oriented Prompts (ToP), are frequently utilized to reinforce safety instructions [Wang_2026_LLM]. However, the effectiveness of these defenses can be highly variable; for instance, few-shot demonstrations have been shown to enhance RoP's safety rate by reinforcing role identity, while simultaneously degrading ToP's effectiveness by distracting attention from task instructions [Wang_2026_LLM].

To address the limitations of static defenses that may degrade model responses to benign prompts or fail to adapt to novel threats, researchers have proposed real-time, self-tuning (RTST) moderator frameworks [Zhang_2025_Real]. These adaptive frameworks defend against modern jailbreaks while maintaining a lightweight training footprint, offering advantages over traditional fine-tuning or static classifier models [Zhang_2025_Real]. Furthermore, the growing integration of LLMs in diverse fields necessitates robust real-time monitoring systems equipped to comprehensively scrutinize outputs and swiftly identify anomalies, data exposure, or illegal content [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking].

Finally, the foundation of secure LLM deployment relies on rigorous red teaming. Internal red-teaming involves synthesizing comprehensive, high-coverage prompts based on real-world tasks to intentionally induce unsafe cyberactivities or harmful outputs during the model's development phase [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. This adversarial data is then utilized in multi-objective reinforcement learning pipelines to optimize model safety and decrease over-refusal rates, ensuring the generation of secure outputs while preserving overall model utility [Liu_2025_Purpcode].

introduction.title: 1. Introduction
introduction.text:
# 1. Introduction

The rapid proliferation and integration of artificial intelligence into critical infrastructure, commercial applications, and daily life have ushered in an era of unprecedented technological capability. However, this widespread adoption has simultaneously exposed a vast and complex attack surface, rendering modern AI systems susceptible to a myriad of adversarial threats. As models have evolved from simple classifiers to sophisticated generative engines, the nature of adversarial attacks has correspondingly transformed in both complexity and severity. This section outlines the foundational context of this survey, detailing the scope of our investigation, the historical and ongoing evolution of the threat landscape, the intense arms race in Large Language Model (LLM) security, and the emerging vulnerabilities inherent in Multimodal AI and Agentic Systems.

### 1.1 Survey Scope

The primary objective of this survey is to provide a comprehensive, systematic, and up-to-date analysis of the adversarial attack landscape targeting modern artificial intelligence systems, with a specific focus on the critical temporal span between 2024 and 2026 [l2_Adversarial Attacks_v2]. This period marks a highly consequential transition in AI security, characterized by the shift from theoretical vulnerabilities to practical, real-world exploits deployed against production-grade systems. 

Our scope encompasses the full spectrum of contemporary AI architectures. We begin by examining the foundational vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), exploring how their reliance on natural language interfaces exposes them to sophisticated prompt injection and jailbreaking techniques. We then extend our analysis to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), investigating how the integration of diverse data modalities—such as vision and audio—creates complex, cross-modal attack vectors. Finally, we explore the frontier of Agentic Systems, where AI models are granted autonomy to execute code, interact with external environments, and utilize tools, thereby dramatically amplifying the potential impact of adversarial compromises. By synthesizing recent literature, this survey aims to equip researchers, practitioners, and policymakers with a holistic understanding of current threats and the state-of-the-art defensive paradigms required to secure the next generation of AI.

### 1.2 Threat Landscape Evolution

The evolution of the adversarial threat landscape is a testament to the adaptive nature of malicious actors in the face of advancing technology. Historically, adversarial machine learning research was predominantly anchored in the computer vision domain, where attacks involved applying imperceptible, continuous perturbations to image pixels to induce misclassification. However, the advent of transformer-based architectures and the subsequent dominance of LLMs necessitated a fundamental shift in adversarial methodologies. 

Today, the threat landscape has migrated from the continuous domain of pixels to the discrete, semantic space of natural language tokens. Prompt-based attacks have emerged as a primary vector, involving the deliberate manipulation of a language model's responses using meticulously engineered malicious prompts [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Because modern LLMs are fundamentally designed to follow user instructions, attackers can exploit this reliance on input prompts to bypass safety filters and coerce the model into producing specific, often harmful, outputs [Yang_2024_Adversarial]. Furthermore, the landscape has expanded beyond inference-time attacks to include sophisticated training-time vulnerabilities, such as data poisoning and the manipulation of reward models used in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [cluster_0]. This evolution signifies a transition from simple evasion tactics to comprehensive systemic compromises, requiring a fundamental rethinking of AI security postures.

### 1.3 The Arms Race in LLM Security

The dynamic between attackers seeking to exploit LLMs and defenders striving to secure them has escalated into a high-stakes, continuous arms race. As developers implement increasingly robust alignment techniques to ensure models remain helpful and harmless, adversaries continuously innovate to circumvent these guardrails. This tension is most visibly manifested in the proliferation of "jailbreak" attacks. 

Recent evaluations of LLM anti-jailbreaking robustness reveal a saturated and highly competitive environment. Attackers have moved beyond simple, manual prompt engineering to deploy sophisticated, automated methodologies. These include template-based attacks utilizing frameworks like H4RM3L, ArtPrompt, and various open-source jailbreak templates, which systematically convert direct malicious requests into obfuscated formats that bypass safety filters [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. Furthermore, adversaries are increasingly leveraging search-based optimization techniques, such as AutoDAN, to algorithmically discover adversarial suffixes or prefixes that reliably trigger restricted behaviors [Liu_2025_Purpcode].

In response, the defensive community is shifting its paradigm. Rather than treating security as an external constraint imposed through rigid prompt filters or post-processing heuristics, recent advancements focus on internalizing security considerations directly into the model's generation process [Thang_2026_LLM]. This involves strengthening secure behaviors as an intrinsic part of the model's alignment, aiming to create systems that are inherently resilient to manipulation rather than merely patched against known exploits. Despite these efforts, the arms race persists, with each defensive innovation inevitably prompting a novel adversarial countermeasure.

### 1.4 Multimodal AI

The pursuit of artificial general intelligence has driven the development of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), which seamlessly integrate visual, auditory, and textual inputs to achieve extraordinary capabilities in comprehension, reasoning, and generation [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. However, this expansion of the model's sensory capabilities inherently broadens its attack surface, introducing complex vulnerabilities that do not exist in unimodal systems.

MLLMs remain highly vulnerable to transferable adversarial examples, where perturbations crafted on a surrogate model successfully deceive a target, black-box model [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. The integration of vision encoders (such as CLIP) with language decoders creates a unique vulnerability: attackers can embed malicious instructions within the visual input itself. While existing defensive methods often focus on aligning global features—such as the CLIP [CLS] token—between adversarial and benign samples, they frequently overlook the rich, localized information encoded in individual patch tokens [Jia_2025_Adversarial]. Adversaries exploit this oversight by crafting adversarial images that appear benign to human observers but force the MLLM to output targeted, malicious text or bypass its safety alignment. The cross-modal nature of these attacks makes them particularly insidious, as defenses must now secure not only the individual modalities but also the complex, high-dimensional interfaces between them.

### 1.5 Agentic Systems

Perhaps the most consequential development in recent AI research is the transition from passive, conversational models to autonomous Agentic Systems. These AI agents—powered by advanced models such as DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, and Gemini [Orel_2026_AI]—are designed to interact with external environments, utilize software tools, and autonomously generate and execute code to achieve complex objectives. While this autonomy unlocks immense utility, it fundamentally alters the risk calculus of adversarial attacks.

When an AI agent is compromised, the impact is no longer confined to the generation of toxic text; it extends to tangible, real-world actions. A critical threat addressed in recent literature arises when an agent, operating under seemingly benign prompts, generates code that is functionally correct but structurally insecure [Thang_2026_LLM]. Adversaries can subtly manipulate the agent's context to induce common vulnerabilities, such as missing input validation when handling external data, unsafe memory management in low-level code, or incomplete authentication logic [Thang_2026_LLM]. Furthermore, prompt injection attacks against agents can lead to "confused deputy" scenarios, where the agent is tricked into executing malicious commands using its own elevated privileges. As Agentic Systems become increasingly integrated into software development pipelines and operational infrastructure, securing them against adversarial manipulation stands as one of the most urgent imperatives in contemporary AI research.
